title: I have won
hook: stake after stake, Shakuni says I have won, and Vidura warns that the winner is in danger too
carry: where dharma is, there is victory

segments.voice: Yesterday, before the first throw: a warning, a dare, a vow, and a pearl set in gold, lost. Keeping a rule isn't the same as dharma.

There's a line in this part of the poem that keeps coming back, like a drumbeat. Yudhishthira names a stake. Shakuni throws. And then Shakuni says, in effect: I have won. Then again. And again. The poem repeats it until the words themselves begin to sound like a warning. And one man in the hall stands up and tries to stop it.
screen: `A LINE LIKE A DRUMBEAT.` → `I HAVE WON.` → `ONE MAN TRIES TO STOP IT.`

segments.voice: After the pearl, Yudhishthira reaches for the next stake. Treasure. Gold. A fine chariot. Servants. Elephants. Horses. Soldiers. Each time he describes the stake carefully, almost proudly. Each time the throw goes to Shakuni, and the same short line follows: I have won. The refrain takes the suspense away. We stop asking who wins the throw, and start asking: why doesn't he stop? Vidura asks it out loud. He turns to the blind king with a picture: a man climbs high after honey, so taken with it that he doesn't see the fall in front of him. That, he says, is your son. Stop the game while there's a family left to save. Duryodhana answers with scorn, and the king says nothing that stops it. Notice: the honey picture isn't about the loser. It's about the winner. Now the teaching. The Mahabharata has a line that comes back again and again, and India's Supreme Court took it as its motto: yato dharmas tato jayah, where dharma is, there is victory. It's the epic's answer to Shakuni's refrain. A throw can be won by trickery. A kingdom can be taken. But in the Hindu view, that isn't victory, because it's won against dharma, and the fruit of it is still coming. Duryodhana's hands are full of honey, and he's walking toward the edge. For today: a win that costs you dharma, a test passed by cheating, an argument won by cruelty, is the kind Vidura warned about. Ask not only did I win, but was dharma with me.
screen: `STAKE AFTER STAKE: I HAVE WON.` · `VIDURA: THE MAN WHO CLIMBS FOR HONEY.` · `THE HONEY IS THE WINNER'S DANGER.` · `YATO DHARMAS TATO JAYAH.` · then, large: `WHERE DHARMA IS, THERE IS VICTORY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that's been going your way lately: a grade, a game, a race at work, an argument. Then do what many Hindus do with a success: offer it. Before you take the credit, set it in your mind at God's feet, or simply say thank you for it, and ask honestly whether it was won with dharma. If anything about it wasn't, let that be your quiet work this week. If you don't pray, offer it to the people who helped you get there.
The dice game. Stake after stake, the same short line, I have won, and an old Hindu answer: where dharma is, there is victory.
Your line: where dharma is, there is victory. Tomorrow, the stakes stop being things. That's day seven hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Vidura's warnings in the dice hall are a place where teachers and storytellers often pause, and his image of the honey-gatherer is retold as a picture of desire that can't see its own danger.

fork.setup: Shakuni has won every throw, and Duryodhana is delighted. Vidura says the winner is the one in danger. why, in the Hindu view?
options: because Shakuni might lose the next throw.
because the win was taken against dharma, and where dharma is, there is victory: the fruit of this win is still coming.
because Vidura secretly wanted the Pandavas to win.
fork.reveal: Vidura's man climbing for honey doesn't see the fall. the epic's answer to 'I have won' is yato dharmas tato jayah: a win against dharma isn't the real victory.

Vidura.meaning: the blind king's half-brother and wise counselor

Dhritarashtra.meaning: the blind king of Hastinapura, Duryodhana's father

Shakuni.meaning: Duryodhana's uncle, a master at dice

Yudhishthira.meaning: eldest of the five Pandava brothers

jaya.meaning: victory; in yato dharmas tato jayah, 'where dharma is, there is victory'
